Chapter 1 opens with this

The one-line change that took a week

“It should have been a one-line change.”

The product owner lowers the annual discount from 20% to 15%. A developer changes the number, runs the tests and deploys. Two days later the checkout page promises one price and the invoice charges another.

Nothing was wrong with the syntax. The same business rule lived in two places, and only one of them received the change. The book starts here, and every chapter adds one more requirement that tests the design.

CheckoutService.javaprice shown
public BigDecimal priceFor(String plan, boolean annual) {
  BigDecimal monthly = switch (plan) {
    case "BASIC" -> new BigDecimal("9.99");
    case "PRO"   -> new BigDecimal("19.99");
    default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(
        "Unknown plan: " + plan);
  };
  if (annual) {
    return monthly.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(12))
        .multiply(new BigDecimal("0.80"))
        .setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
  }
  return monthly;
}
InvoiceService.javaprice charged
public BigDecimal amountDue(Subscription subscription) {
  BigDecimal monthly = subscription.getPlan().equals("PRO")
      ? new BigDecimal("19.99")
      : new BigDecimal("9.99");   // unknown plan? Basic
  if (subscription.isAnnual()) {
    return monthly.multiply(new BigDecimal("12"))
        .multiply(new BigDecimal("0.8"))
        .setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
  }
  return monthly;
}

2 copies of one pricing rule, already disagreeing about unknown plans.

PricingPolicy.javathe only home of the rule
public class PricingPolicy {
  private static final BigDecimal ANNUAL_DISCOUNT =
      new BigDecimal("0.15");
  private static final int MONTHS_PER_YEAR = 12;

  public BigDecimal priceFor(Plan plan, BillingCycle cycle) {
    if (cycle == BillingCycle.MONTHLY) {
      return plan.monthlyPrice();
    }
    BigDecimal fullYear = plan.monthlyPrice()
        .multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(MONTHS_PER_YEAR));
    return fullYear
        .multiply(BigDecimal.ONE.subtract(ANNUAL_DISCOUNT))
        .setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);
  }
}
CheckoutService.java · InvoiceService.javaboth ask
public BigDecimal priceFor(Plan plan, BillingCycle cycle) {
  return pricing.priceFor(plan, cycle);
}

public BigDecimal amountDue(Subscription subscription) {
  return pricing.priceFor(subscription.plan(),
                          subscription.cycle());
}

1 line to change the discount. An unknown plan cannot even reach the pricing code.

One system, eleven chapters

Every principle arrives when a real requirement needs it

You follow SubFlow, a subscription-billing service, from a procedural first version to a tested, modular system with a public API, two payment providers and prices that marketing changes without a deployment. The requirements are ordinary. That is the point: you will meet every one of them at work.

How each principle is taught

The whole picture, including the part most books skip

DRY, KISS, YAGNI, coupling and cohesion, SOLID, testability, boundaries and architecture all follow the same ten steps. Steps 7 and 8 are the reason this book exists: a principle applied without judgment can make code worse, so each one comes with its costs and with the cases where you should not use it.

Chapter 5 then puts principles against each other, DRY against simplicity or reuse against independent evolution, and gives you the questions that settle the argument.

About the author

Moises Gamio

A software engineer with more than twenty-five years of experience building business systems in banking, government, retail, e-commerce and business-to-business integration. Most of that time he worked in companies where software was not the product but the tool that sells, bills and delivers. This book is about the design decisions working developers make under real deadlines.

He writes about software design and architecture at codersite.dev. The first edition of this book, Software Design Principles: A Practical Guide, was published in 2022.

Questions

Before you buy

I don’t write Java. Is it for me?
Yes. The examples use plain Java 17 because it reads clearly, but the principles apply equally to C#, Kotlin, TypeScript, Python and other languages. No framework knowledge is needed.
I read the first edition. What is new?
Everything was rewritten around one growing system, and there are four new chapters: testability, conflicting principles, boundaries and APIs, and architecture. UML became a chapter on communicating design, and four appendices were added.
Where is the code?
On GitHub at github.com/mgamio/subFlow, one Maven module per chapter, with the “before” versions kept next to the refactored ones and tests that prove the behavior stayed the same.
Paperback or Kindle?
The paperback is 6 × 9 inches with figures and code printed for reading on paper. The Kindle edition has the same content, with linked chapters for reading on any device.
